title: The feasibility of virtual reality (VR)-enhanced cue exposure therapy versus neutral VR exposure for cocaine use disorder, with wearable monitoring and timely check-ins in everyday life
official: A randomised feasibility trial of VR-enhanced cue exposure therapy versus neutral VR exposure for cocaine use disorder, with wearable monitoring and JITA-EMA
summary:
Background and study aims 
Craving for cocaine can be triggered by many things, including places, people, emotions and everyday situations. Stress can also increase craving and make it harder to stay in control. Talking therapies (for example, cognitive behavioural approaches) can help, but relapse is common and craving can still be difficult to manage in day-to-day life. Virtual Reality (VR) can recreate realistic situations in a safe clinic setting. The study compares two VR approaches to managing craving: one that exposes people to cocaine‑related cues in VR to help them practise coping skills, and another that uses calming VR environments to reduce stress and manage stress‑related craving.

This is a feasibility study. That means it is testing whether the study procedures work (for example, recruitment, attendance and follow-up), and whether both types of VR can be delivered safely and are acceptable in services. It will also collect early information to help plan a larger future study.

Who can participate? 
Adult patients aged 18 years and over who are seeking treatment for cocaine substance use disorder.

What does the study involve? 
This study will compare two VR-based approaches that may help people manage craving in different ways.
•	VR-enhanced Cue Exposure Therapy (VR-CET): uses VR cocaine-related situations to help people practise coping with cravings triggered by cues (for example, environments or social situations linked to use).
•	VR-Relaxation: uses calming VR environments to help reduce stress and practise strategies that may reduce stress-related craving.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Possible benefits of taking part: While it cannot be guaranteed that there will be any specific treatment benefits from taking part, research does deliver wider benefits to society and future treatment options for those undergoing substance use treatment. 

Possible risks of taking part: 
VR motion sickness: Some people experience motion sickness in VR. To minimise this, the amount of movement within the VR scenarios has been reduced with regular breaks scheduled. Participants can also stop if they start to feel unwell or for any other reason. 
Sensitive topics: Participants will complete an interview, which will ask about cocaine use and the experience of viewing the cocaine scenarios. This may lead them to think about sensitive topics or memories. Participants will be aware that they can stop at any point and that there is no right answer.  
Craving: The VR-CET cues all involve triggers which may induce cocaine craving. To reduce this effect, before leaving the setting, participants will remain until their craving returns to baseline. They will also be provided with a coping with craving handout to go through with participants and for them to take home to support craving reduction. Participants can stay with the researcher at the service until they feel able to leave.  

Where is the study run from?  
King's College London, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN), UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
July 2026 to July 2027.

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prof Paolo Deluca, paolo.deluca@kcl.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Treatment-seeking patients for cocaine SUD
2. Able and willing to provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Evidence of severe mental illness or cognitive impairment
2. Impaired vision or hearing that cannot be corrected (i.e. with contact lenses, glasses or hearing aid)
3. Physical inability to wear a wrist device
4. Both arms having tattoo sleeves (as the device requires contact with ink-free skin)
5. Current participation in a similar research study
